items.claim: A submitted field that the framework silently discards — because it is absent from the model's fillable list — is not a mass-assignment finding; the mass-assignment defect requires the unexpected field to actually change persisted state or a privilege-bearing attribute.
items.disproof: The rule is wrong when the discarded-attribute behaviour is a development-only diagnostic that is switched off in production, or when the framework logs and then applies the attribute on a different code path (a fillable check that is bypassed for nested JSON keys, or a direct column write outside the mass-assignment call), in which case the same request that looks discarded in one flow mutates state in another.

sources.quote: By default, attributes that are not included in the Fillable attribute are silently discarded when performing mass-assignment operations.
When adding extra fields to the form, you can also use the getExtraData() method to get any submitted data that doesn't correspond to a form field.

items.body: Mechanism: A submitted field that the framework silently discards — because it is absent from the model's fillable list — is not a mass-assignment finding; the mass-assignment defect requires the unexpected field to actually change persisted state or a privilege-bearing attribute. How to apply it in the field: treat this as the fp_rule it is — a hunter must be able to state the concrete observation that demonstrates it, with a request and response in hand, before the finding is reportable. Boundary of the rule: The rule is wrong when the discarded-attribute behaviour is a development-only diagnostic that is switched off in production, or when the framework logs and then applies the attribute on a different code path (a fillable check that is bypassed for nested JSON keys, or a direct column write outside the mass-assignment call), in which case the same request that looks discarded in one flow mutates state in another.

items.claim: A convincing mass-assignment proof is a successful response paired with a readback showing the privileged field changed — a follow-up GET, or the object returned by the same request echoing the new value — because a 2xx on its own does not show the attribute reached the database.
items.disproof: The claim is false when the endpoint has no read path available to the tester and the response body never echoes model state; there the evidence must come from an out-of-band channel (a second account observing the change, an email or webhook triggered by the field, or a database log), and without one the finding is unproven rather than disproven.

sources.quote: A mass assignment vulnerability occurs when a user passes an unexpected HTTP request field and that field changes a column in your database that you did not expect.
The submission of extra form fields can be controlled with the allow_extra_fields config option

items.claim: An API that accepts a body containing fields it does not know is not automatically vulnerable: the finding only exists once a submitted field maps to a server-side attribute the caller must not control, typically an ownership, role, price or verification flag.
items.disproof: The rule is wrong when the ignored field is not simply inert — for example it feeds a logging/audit sink, a cache key, a search index, a downstream webhook payload, or a denormalised duplicate used for authorisation — in which case the same unexpected field is already attacker-controlled and produces an effect even without touching the protected column.

sources.quote: These attributes are required because all Eloquent models are protected against mass assignment vulnerabilities by default.

items.claim: A fillable/guarded allowlist is only a defence as strong as its contents: because the allowlist is an explicit enumeration of attribute names, a single over-broad entry (a whole table of columns, a prefix pattern, or a nested JSON path that includes a privileged sub-key) re-opens mass assignment without weakening the mechanism itself.
items.disproof: The rule is false when the privileged field is stored in a different model or table from the allowlisted one, or when the ORM writes it through a dedicated setter that the mass-assignment path never reaches, so the over-broad entry still cannot set it.

items.claim: A model marked unguarded, or a controller that hand-builds the array passed to the ORM's create/update call from the raw request, is a far stronger mass-assignment signal than a generic `role` key in a request body, because it identifies the specific code path with no allowlist at all.
items.disproof: The claim is false when the unguarded model is a value object or DTO that never persists a privilege-bearing column, or when every value in the hand-built array is read from a server-side constant and merged with a validated subset of the request; the marker is then present but the sink is not attacker-reachable.

sources.quote: If you choose to unguard your model, you should take special care to always hand-craft the arrays passed to Eloquent's fill , create , and update methods:
